Basal metabolic rate in Miller's long-tongued bat, Glossophaga longirostris, has been measured at 26.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 26.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animals are resting under thermoneutral conditions, specifically at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This relatively modest oxygen consumption for a neotropical nectarivore reflects the species' efficient energy budgeting, as individuals must frequently alternate between periods of high activity during foraging bouts and extended periods of torpor when food resources are scarce. The value was obtained from respirometry trials conducted on post-absorptive adults and is consistent with the general pattern observed among glossophagine bats, which tend to exhibit lower mass-specific metabolic rates compared to insectivorous species of comparable body size.

Neonatal pups of Glossophaga longirostris emerge weighing approximately 4.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.5 grams], a birth mass that represents a substantial proportion of the mother's post-partum body weight and underscores the high energetic investment per offspring characteristic of this phyllostomid lineage. This altricial newborn is entirely dependent on maternal milk during its initial weeks of life, with the suckling juvenile gradually transitioning to a diet of nectar and pollen as it approaches independence. Under typical conditions, the nursing offspring remains tightly attached to the mother's ventral fur for the first several days, a behavior that facilitates thermoregulation and reduces the energetic demands of maintaining a stable core temperature during a period of rapid somatic growth.

The gestational period for Glossophaga longirostris lasts approximately 90 days [tg = approximately 90 days] when pregnancies are maintained at a core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that is fairly typical for a bat of this size within the subfamily Glossophaginae. Following parturition, the female enters a postpartum estrus and can produce up to two litters per year [F_R_i = up to two litters per year], with each litter consisting of a single pup [N_R_i = each litter consisting of a single pup]. This reproductive strategy, combining a modest gestation length with a relatively high annual fecundity for a bat, allows the species to capitalize on seasonal floral resource pulses across its Neotropical range, where nectar availability can vary dramatically between wet and dry seasons.

At a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], sexual maturation in this species, defined as the attainment of full gonadal functionality, occurs at 280 days after birth [tp = 280 days after birth]. This relatively rapid progression to reproductive maturity, roughly 9 to 10 months of age, enables young adults born early in the rainy season to participate in the subsequent breeding window. The weaning process, which marks the end of the suckling juvenile phase, concludes at approximately 30.5 days after birth [tx = approximately 30.5 days after birth], a value inferred from comparative data on the congener A at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]noura caudifer. By this stage, the young bat has developed sufficient flight musculature and foraging skills to begin exploiting local nectar sources independently, though some maternal association may persist during the early post-weaning period.

Adult body mass in Glossophaga longirostris exhibits a modest degree of sexual dimorphism, with females attaining an ultimate wet weight of 12.81 grams [Wwi = 12.81 grams] while males reach a slightly heavier average of 13.25 grams [Wwi = 13.25 grams]. Maximum lifespan in this species, based on longevity records extrapolated from the ecologically similar Anoura caudifer, is estimated at approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when maintained at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This decade-long lifespan is comparatively extended for a mammal of this small body size and is likely linked to the low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by roosting in stable cave environments and a foraging strategy that relies on abundant, predictable floral resources. The combination of a relatively long life, moderate reproductive output, and directed parental investment places this nectarivorous bat firmly within the slow end of the fast-slow life-history continuum for Neotropical mammals.
